paras: Harbrook Systems is a vendor that sells software to manufacturers. We do not sell to retail, to banks or to public bodies, and we are asked about it often enough that we now say it on this page: we specialize in one industry, and we refuse everything else. The companies we serve make things in factories, and they all have the same problem on a Monday morning.

The company, which was founded in 2009 by two former plant managers, launched its current platform in 2019 and rebuilt it twice after that. Our headquarters is in Utrecht, where ninety of our people work, and our second office is in Munich. Germany is the market where we earn most of our revenue, and it is also the market where we lose most of our deals, which tells you something about how crowded it is.

Our Brazilian operation is not an office. It is a subsidiary of a local partner who has been with us since 2016, and it serves eleven accounts in the south of the country. That is the whole footprint: two offices, one partner, and a list of customers that is shorter than our competitors like to mention.

The person who answers this page is a real one. If you write to us, you will hear back from somebody in the commercial team within two working days, and that person will have read what you sent. We do not run a contact form that goes nowhere.

items.situation: The page says the company sells to manufacturers only. Say that in one sentence with a relative clause and no comma.
tips: They are a vendor that sells only to manufacturers.
The clause says which kind of vendor, so no comma.

items.situation: Add the founding year to this sentence as extra information: Harbrook is based in Utrecht.
tips: Harbrook, which was founded in 2009, is based in Utrecht.
Two commas, and never that after a comma.

items.situation: Somebody says: Utrecht is the city that they have their headquarters there. What is wrong, and what is right?
tips: Utrecht is the city where they have their headquarters.
Where already carries in which, so there is no second there.

items.situation: You want to ask about the decision maker. Build the question with two relative words.
tips: Who is the person who decides which vendors you work with?
Who for the person, which for the vendors.

items.situation: The page says the footprint is two offices and one partner. Say what a footprint is, in your own words.
tips: All the places where a company operates, seen together.
Not the size of the company -- the reach of it.

items.situation: Turn one fact from the page into an opening question for the call.
tips: I saw that Germany is where you earn most of your revenue. Is it also where the hardest deals are?
One fact, one question. Never a list.

listenings.text: I give myself ten minutes before a first call, and I look for three things, always in the same order. First, who they sell to. Not what they sell, who they sell to, because that tells me whether we have anything in common. Second, what changed in the last year. A new office, a new product, a new person in a senior role, anything that gives me a reason to be curious. Third, the person who will be on the call, because a partner manager and an engineer need completely different conversations. I stopped reading product pages years ago. Every product page in this industry says the same four things, and none of them tell me anything about that particular company. And here is the part people get wrong: I never recite what I found. Nothing kills a first call faster than a stranger reading your own website back to you. I turn one fact into one question, and then I stop talking.

There is a sentence at the top of our own company page, and I want to be honest about it: nobody has ever said that sentence out loud. Not me, not the sales team, not the person who wrote it, and a lawyer and a marketing agency wrote it together, which explains a lot. When I describe the same company at a dinner, it comes out completely differently. I say we work with factories that cannot tell you on Friday what they produced on Monday, and everybody at the table understands immediately, because everybody has worked somewhere that was a bit like that. So my advice, when you read a company page before a call, is simple. Read it for the facts and never for the words. Take the numbers, take the names, take the markets and the dates. Then throw the adjectives away, because they were not written to tell you anything.
